title: 「強い宰相」の発信スタイル　高市首相、生活不安を払拭できるか
extracted_text:
「強い」イメージを前面に掲げるべきだ――。半年ほど前に高市早苗政権が船出した際、首相周辺は危機管理に堂々と臨む姿を意識的に打ち出すよう進言したという。

その実践の一つが外交・安全保障についての積極的な発信だった。「外出の予定を変更して、いま状況の報告を受けた」。首相就任の翌朝、北朝鮮が短距離弾道ミサイルを発射すると、首相は閣僚に先駆けて自ら記者団にこう強調した。

自民党が2月の衆院選に大勝した後も基本路線は変わらない。施政方針演説は国力強化を軸に据えた。「外交力、防衛力、経済力、技術力、情報力、そして人材力」と外交、防衛を前に出して「力」という言葉を並べた。

首相の姿勢は時代の動きにはまったといえるかもしれない。世論調査で優先処理してほしい政策を複数回答で聞いた際に「外交・安保」を挙げる割合が高まっている。

菅義偉政権では平均22%、岸田文雄政権は23%、石破茂政権は24%だった。ウクライナ侵略やパレスチナ自治区ガザの衝突が始まった直後の月も3割を超えてはいなかった。これが高市政権下の2025年10月以降は平均で31%に上昇した。

永田町では長らく「外交・安保は票にならない」といわれてきた。足元の変化の背景には何があるのだろうか。

昨秋、首相の台湾有事に関する国会答弁に中国が反発し、自国民に日本への渡航自粛を求めた。日本企業への輸出規制を強化し、レアアース（希土類）などの供給が途絶える懸念が身近な話題になった。

2月末には米国やイスラエルの攻撃を受けたイランがホルムズ海峡を事実上封鎖した。日本も中東湾岸地域からの原油供給が途絶えるリスクに直面している。燃油相場の高騰は身近な生活物資の値上げを招く。

今回の国際的な緊張は「遠い世界の出来事」でない。中東情勢への対応は生活を左右する政策として継続的に関心を集めている。

かつて田中角栄元首相は「政治とは生活である」と語った。2000年代には民主党が「国民の生活が第一」を掲げて政権を獲得した。今も優先処理を望む政策のトップは物価対策だ。

日本社会の目下の関心は中東情勢によって原油や石油関連製品の供給が途絶えないかという点だろう。首相は4月上旬、自らのX（旧ツイッター）に不安の打ち消しを図るメッセージを相次いで投稿した。

8カ月分の石油備蓄があると発信し、供給不安の見方が流れたナフサについても国内需要4カ月分を確保していると強調した。

7日には記者団に「年を越えて供給を確保できるめどがついた」と話し、以前よりも供給可能な時期が延びていることを示した。

首相の発信による効果かは不明だが、石油関連製品の買い占めがあちこちで起きるような混乱は起きていない。一方で、企業や国民の懸念を払拭できているわけでもない。

首相の発信はXを多用するスタイルだ。タイムリーに情報を流せる半面、一方的な発信になりがちな面がある。7日は記者団の前で話す「ぶら下がり取材」の形式だったが、受け付けた質問は2つだった。

首相の発言を踏まえて追加質問を重ねられる記者会見の回数は菅、岸田、石破各首相と比べて少ない。一問一答形式の予算審議への出席時間も最近の政権に比べて短かった。

広がっている不安を払拭するには疑問が解消されるまで質問に答えるのが一つの方法となる。それは「強い宰相」を印象づけることにもつながるのではないだろうか。（宮坂正太郎）

【コラム「風見鶏」最近の5本】
translated_text:
They should put the "strong" image in the foreground. When the Takachi administration launched about half a year ago, those close to the prime minister allegedly advised her to deliberately project a stance of facing crisis management head-on.

One example of this practice was proactive communication on foreign affairs and security. "I changed my schedule to go out and received a situation report right now." The morning after she became prime minister, when North Korea launched a short-range ballistic missile, the prime minister emphasized this to reporters before the cabinet ministers.

The basic course has not changed even after the Liberal Democratic Party's big victory in the February general election. Her policy speech was centered on strengthening national power. She listed "diplomatic power, defense power, economic power, technology power, information power, and human resources" by placing foreign affairs and defense at the front and arranging the word "power."

The prime minister's stance may well be in tune with the times. When surveys asked respondents to choose multiple policies they wanted prioritized, the percentage citing "foreign affairs and security" has been increasing.

Under the Suga administration it averaged 22%, the Kishida administration 23%, and the Ishiba administration 24%. Even in the months immediately after the start of the Ukraine invasion and the Gaza conflict, it never exceeded 30%. Since October 2025 under the Takachi administration, it has risen to an average of 31%.

In Nagatacho, it has long been said that "foreign affairs and security don't win votes." What lies behind this change?

Last fall, China's retaliation against the prime minister's Diet responses regarding a Taiwan contingency and its request for citizens to refrain from traveling to Japan became a familiar topic. Strengthening export regulations on Japanese companies and concerns about supplies of rare earths becoming interrupted became everyday topics.

At the end of February, Iran, attacked by the US and Israel, effectively closed the Hormuz Strait. Japan also faces the risk of crude oil supplies from the Gulf region being interrupted. Soaring fuel prices are causing everyday necessities to increase in price.

This international tension is not a "faraway world event." Response to Middle East situations is continuously gaining interest as a policy that affects daily life.

Former Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka once said, "Politics is about livelihood." In the 2000s, the Democratic Party captured power by declaring "People's livelihood first." The top policy people want prioritized now is measures against rising prices.

Current interest in Japanese society likely centers on whether crude oil and petroleum product supplies will not be interrupted due to Middle East situations. In early April, the prime minister posted successive messages on her X (formerly Twitter) aimed at dispelling anxieties.

She emphasized that there are eight months of petroleum reserves and that she has secured four months' worth of domestic demand for naphtha, which had concerns about supply shortages.

On the 7th, she told reporters, "We have secured supply prospects beyond the year," showing that the period of possible supply has been extended compared to before.


While it is unclear whether the effect is due to her communication, there has been no widespread confusion such as hoarding of petroleum products in various places. On the other hand, concerns among businesses and citizens have not been completely dispelled.

The prime minister's communication style makes frequent use of X. While it can disseminate information in a timely manner, it tends to become one-sided communication. On the 7th, it was in the form of a "doorstop interview" where she spoke in front of reporters, but only two questions were taken.

The number of press conferences where follow-up questions were asked based on the prime minister's statements is fewer compared to Prime Ministers Suga, Kishida, and Ishiba. The time spent answering questions in the budget examination in a Q&A format was also shorter than in recent administrations.

One way to dispel growing anxieties is to continue answering questions until doubts are resolved. Could that also help leave an impression of a "strong prime minister"? (Masataro Miyasaka)

title_en: "Strong Prime Minister" Communication Style - Can PM Takachi Eliminate Public Anxiety Over Living Costs?
